uncited: It distinguishes itself from sibling methods like [Gaussian Frosting Layer Creation](12579-gaussian-frosting-layer-creation.md) and [Dual-Domain Deformation Model](12804-dual-domain-deformation-model.md) by explicitly supervising the SDF gradient direction against monocular normal estimates to ensure the Gaussians represent a coherent surface rather than a volumetric density field.
The scene is represented by a set of $N$ 3D Gaussians.
**Rasterization and Rendering:** Project the 3D Gaussians onto the 2D image plane as splats.
**Adaptive Density Control:** Interleave optimization with adaptive density control.
Add new Gaussians to "empty" areas (missing geometric features) or areas where a single Gaussian covers a large part of the scene.
*   Rasterize the projected gradient values to the corresponding pixel positions using the GS rasterizer.
Repeat steps 2-9 for the training iterations.
*   **Semi-transparent Gaussians:** Standard GS optimization may result in semi-transparent Gaussians which are undesirable for mesh extraction.
*   **Monocular Normal Accuracy:** The quality of the normal regularization depends on the accuracy of the pretrained monocular normal estimator (e.g., Omnidata, MiDaS).
*   **SDF Estimation:** The SDF is estimated from depth maps.
*   **Parameter Tuning:** The weight $\lambda_r$ needs to be tuned per scene.
*   **Time Complexity:** The method adds the overhead of monocular normal estimation and SDF gradient computation to the standard GS optimization.
*   **Memory Complexity:** Requires storing additional data for SDF gradients and monocular normals.
*   Use when high-quality surface mesh extraction is required from 2D images.
*   Use standard GS if mesh extraction is not required and photometric quality is the sole metric.
The method builds upon the original 3D Gaussian Splatting paper [1] and addresses its limitations in geometry reconstruction.
